title: Development of the Kidneys and Urinary Tract
subject: Renal and Urinary System (RENL)

overview.intro: This chapter follows the urinary system from intermediate mesoderm to a working kidney, ureter, bladder, and urethra. It covers the three successive kidneys, the reciprocal induction that builds nephrons and collecting ducts, renal ascent, ureteric bud splitting, partition of the cloaca, and the fate of the allantois. Board questions usually name one finding, such as oligohydramnios, urine at the umbilicus, a low fused kidney, or constant dribbling in a girl, and ask which developmental step failed. Each anomaly in this chapter follows directly from a normal step, so learning the sequence lets you predict the defect rather than memorize it.
prerequisites: Trilaminar disc and the subdivisions of mesoderm (paraxial, intermediate, lateral plate)

connections.how: The mesonephric duct that gives rise to the ureteric bud becomes the male genital ducts, and the urogenital sinus forms both the bladder and parts of the reproductive tract.
Lung growth depends on adequate amniotic fluid, so failure of fetal urine output causes pulmonary hypoplasia.
The adult arrangement of calyces, collecting ducts, renal arteries, and the trigone reflects the embryonic origin of each part.

connections.to: Urinary tract infection and reflux nephropathy
connections.how: Short intravesical ureters and obstructed drainage from developmental errors set up stasis, reflux, ascending infection, and scarring.
Mutations in genes that control induction, such as RET and WT1, and syndromes such as Turner syndrome, link single genes and karyotype to renal anomalies.

sections.title: Three kidneys in sequence: pronephros, mesonephros, metanephros

blocks.text: The urinary system arises from intermediate mesoderm, the strip of mesoderm between the somites and the lateral plate. As the embryo folds, this tissue separates from the somites and forms a longitudinal ridge on each side of the posterior body wall, the nephrogenic cord. Three kidney systems form from this cord in a head to tail order, and the timing overlaps, so the cranial system regresses while the next one develops below it.

The pronephros appears early in the fourth week in the future neck as a few solid cell clusters or vestigial tubules. It never filters blood in humans and is gone by the end of the fourth week. The mesonephros appears in the thoracic and lumbar region late in the fourth week, as the pronephros regresses. Its tubules acquire a capillary tuft at their medial end, forming a true glomerulus inside a Bowman capsule, and their lateral ends drain into the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct, which runs caudally to open into the cloaca. The mesonephros may produce small amounts of urine as an interim kidney, then largely degenerates by the end of the second month.

The mesonephric duct matters long after its kidney fails, for two reasons. First, in the fifth week it sprouts the ureteric bud, which starts the permanent kidney. Second, in males under testosterone the duct persists, and a few mesonephric tubules near the testis become the efferent ductules, while the duct forms the epididymis, ductus deferens, seminal vesicle, and ejaculatory duct; in females they leave only small remnants such as Gartner duct cysts. This shared origin is why urinary and genital anomalies often occur together.

blocks.title: The three kidney systems
rows: Permanent kidney; urine from about weeks 10 to 12
Mostly gone by end of month 2; duct persists
Ureteric bud from the duct; male genital ducts
Nephrons and, with the bud, the collecting system
blocks.caption: Each system arises from intermediate mesoderm caudal to the last; only the metanephros survives as a kidney.

blocks.text: The metanephros, the permanent kidney, appears in the fifth week in the sacral region from two sources described in the next section: the ureteric bud and the metanephric mesenchyme at the caudal end of the nephrogenic cord. It begins producing urine at about weeks 10 to 12. That urine passes into the amniotic cavity, and from about the middle of pregnancy fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid. The fetus does not need its kidneys for excretion, because the placenta clears waste, but it does need their urine to maintain amniotic fluid volume. This distinction explains why a fetus without kidneys can grow to term with normal blood chemistry yet be born with lungs too small to survive.

New nephrons continue to form until about weeks 34 to 36, when nephrogenesis ends; no new nephrons are made after that, although existing ones enlarge and mature after birth. A term infant has roughly one million nephrons per kidney, with wide individual variation. Preterm birth, growth restriction, or obstruction during this window can therefore leave a permanently reduced nephron number.

sections.title: Reciprocal induction: collecting system and nephron

blocks.text: The permanent kidney forms only when two tissues meet. In the fifth week the ureteric bud grows dorsally from the caudal mesonephric duct, near its entry into the cloaca, and pushes into the metanephric mesenchyme, which condenses around its tip as a cap. Neither tissue can build a kidney alone, and each instructs the other, which is why the process is called reciprocal induction.

blocks.title: Reciprocal induction between bud and mesenchyme
steps: WT1 makes the mesenchyme competent to respond
Mesenchyme secretes GDNF, which binds RET on the bud
Bud tip grows and branches into the mesenchyme
Bud tips secrete WNT9B and FGF signals
Mesenchyme condenses and survives around each new tip
Condensed mesenchyme keeps secreting GDNF
blocks.caption: Each bud branch induces new nephrons, and the induced mesenchyme drives further branching.

blocks.text: The ureteric bud forms the collecting system, the passages that carry finished urine. Its stalk becomes the ureter and its expanded tip the renal pelvis. The tip divides repeatedly: the first generations of branches form the major calyces, the next few coalesce into minor calyces, and later generations elongate into the collecting ducts and papillary ducts of the medulla.

The metanephric mesenchyme forms the nephron, the part that makes urine. Around each new collecting duct tip, mesenchymal cells condense and undergo a mesenchyme to epithelium transition, forming a renal vesicle that becomes a comma shaped and then an S shaped tubule. Capillaries invade one end, which folds around them as the double walled Bowman capsule with podocytes on its inner layer. The tubule then lengthens into the proximal convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, and distal convoluted tubule, and its distal end fuses with the adjacent collecting duct. The boundary between the two tissues therefore lies at the junction of the distal convoluted tubule with the collecting duct.

blocks.title: Embryonic origin of adult kidney parts
rows: Ureter, renal pelvis, major and minor calyces, collecting ducts
Bowman capsule (including podocytes), proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal convoluted tubule
blocks.caption: Plumbing comes from the bud; the filtering and processing nephron comes from the mesenchyme.

blocks.text: If the bud fails to form, fails to reach the mesenchyme, or cannot respond to GDNF (for example with loss of function RET variants), no branching occurs, the unstimulated mesenchyme dies by apoptosis, and no kidney forms. This is renal agenesis. Partial or disordered induction instead produces renal dysplasia, a kidney of cysts and primitive tubules with little function. Unilateral agenesis is usually silent: the single kidney enlarges by compensatory hypertrophy, the ipsilateral ureter is absent, and genital duct anomalies may accompany it because the mesonephric duct is shared.
Bilateral agenesis means no fetal urine, and lung growth fails because it needs surrounding amniotic fluid.

blocks.title: Bilateral renal agenesis to Potter sequence
steps: Ureteric buds absent or fail to induce mesenchyme
No nephrons, so no fetal urine
Oligohydramnios from the second trimester
Uterine compression: flat face, low set ears, limb deformities
Too little fluid for lung growth: pulmonary hypoplasia
Respiratory failure at birth
blocks.caption: The fatal problem is pulmonary hypoplasia, not uremia, because the placenta handles excretion before birth.

blocks.predict: A fetus has bilateral renal agenesis. What would its serum creatinine be just before birth, and why does it still die soon after delivery?
blocks.explain: Creatinine is near the maternal value because the placenta clears waste; death follows from pulmonary hypoplasia caused by oligohydramnios, with renal failure developing only after the cord is cut.

sections.title: Ascent of the kidneys, pelvic kidney, and horseshoe kidney

blocks.text: The metanephros forms in the pelvis, with its hilum facing forward. Between about weeks 6 and 9 it comes to lie in the upper lumbar region against the suprarenal gland. This ascent is mostly relative: the lumbar and sacral parts of the body grow rapidly and the body curvature lessens, so the caudal body grows away from the kidneys. During ascent each kidney rotates medially by about 90 degrees, so the hilum comes to face anteromedially.

As the kidneys rise, they are supplied in turn by arteries arising from progressively higher levels: first branches near the common iliac arteries, then successively higher aortic branches. The lower vessels normally regress as new ones arise above. A vessel that fails to regress remains as an accessory renal artery, which is common (about one person in four). Each is an end artery to its segment, so ligation or occlusion causes infarction of that segment, and an accessory vessel to the lower pole that crosses in front of the ureter can compress it and cause hydronephrosis.

On their way up, the kidneys pass through the narrow fork formed by the umbilical arteries. If one kidney fails to pass, it stays in the pelvis near the common iliac artery as a pelvic kidney, supplied by low vessels, often malrotated, and with a short ureter. If the two are pressed together in the fork, their lower poles fuse across the midline, producing a horseshoe kidney, the most common renal fusion anomaly (roughly 1 in 400 to 1 in 600 people).

blocks.title: Formation of a horseshoe kidney
steps: Both kidneys pass through the umbilical arterial fork
Lower poles meet and fuse across the midline
Isthmus lies in front of the aorta and IVC
Isthmus catches under the root of the inferior mesenteric artery
Ascent stops; kidneys stay low in the lumbar region
Fused poles block normal medial rotation
blocks.caption: The inferior mesenteric artery, arising from the aorta at about L3, is the structure that halts ascent of the fused kidney.

blocks.text: The fused isthmus, made of functioning renal tissue or fibrous tissue, lies anterior to the aorta and inferior vena cava. When the rising kidney reaches the inferior mesenteric artery, the isthmus hooks beneath it and cannot pass, so the kidneys remain at about the level of the lower lumbar vertebrae. The superior mesenteric artery arises higher and is not involved. Because rotation also fails, the renal pelves face forward and the ureters must pass anterior to the isthmus, which kinks them at the ureteropelvic junction.

Most horseshoe kidneys cause no symptoms and are found incidentally, and renal function is usually normal. The complications follow from the anatomy: angled, high inserting ureters drain poorly, so ureteropelvic junction obstruction, hydronephrosis, stasis, stones, and infection are more frequent. The low position anterior to the spine also makes the isthmus vulnerable to blunt abdominal trauma. Horseshoe kidney is associated with Turner syndrome (45,X), trisomy 18, and a modestly higher risk of Wilms tumor, so its discovery should prompt attention to these associations.

blocks.caption: Each anomaly corresponds to one failed part of ascent: movement, vessel regression, separation, or rotation.

sections.title: Bifid and duplex ureters, ectopic orifices, obstruction, and reflux

blocks.text: Ureteral duplication is one of the most common congenital anomalies of the urinary tract. Its form depends on when and how the ureteric bud divides. If a single bud splits early, before it enters the metanephric mesenchyme, the two branches drain separate upper and lower parts of the kidney but join to form one ureter before the bladder: a bifid (partial) ureter with one orifice. If two separate buds arise from the mesonephric duct, each forms a complete ureter with its own orifice: a duplex (complete) ureter. In both, the kidney has upper and lower pole moieties, each with its own pelvis.

Where each ureteric orifice ends up follows from how the caudal mesonephric duct is absorbed into the developing bladder wall. As the duct is taken up, the ureteric bud acquires its own opening into the bladder and is carried upward and laterally, while the duct remnant moves downward toward the urethra. In a complete duplication, the bud that arises closer to the bladder (which drains the lower pole) is absorbed first and is carried farther upward and laterally. The bud that arises higher on the duct (which drains the upper pole) is absorbed later, stays with the duct longer, and opens lower and more medially, sometimes outside the bladder altogether. This relationship is the Weigert-Meyer rule.

blocks.title: Complete ureteral duplication (Weigert-Meyer rule)
rows: Long, or orifice ectopic outside the trigone
Hydroureteronephrosis of the upper pole, often dysplastic
Recurrent infection and scarring of the lower pole
blocks.caption: The two ureters cross as they descend, so the upper pole ureter ends lower in the urinary tract.

blocks.text: Reflux and obstruction are opposite failures of the ureterovesical junction. Normally the ureter runs obliquely through the bladder wall in a long submucosal tunnel; as the bladder fills and contracts, its pressure flattens this tunnel and acts as a flap valve that prevents backflow. A laterally placed lower pole orifice has a short, straight tunnel, so the valve fails and urine refluxes into the ureter during voiding, carrying bacteria to the renal pelvis and causing pyelonephritis and reflux scarring. An upper pole orifice that ends low or ectopically often has a narrowed opening or a ureterocele, a cystic dilation of the terminal ureter, and the result is obstruction and dilation of that moiety.

An ectopic ureter opens outside its normal site on the trigone, and the clinical result depends on sex because the possible sites differ. In a girl the orifice can lie below the external urethral sphincter, in the distal urethra, vestibule, or vagina, so urine from that moiety leaks continuously while she also voids normally from the bladder. In a boy, ectopic orifices stay on derivatives of the mesonephric duct or the urethra above the external sphincter (bladder neck, prostatic urethra, seminal vesicle, ductus deferens, or ejaculatory duct), so boys are not incontinent but may present with infection, obstruction, or epididymitis.

blocks.title: Worked example: dribbling with normal voiding
blocks.text: A 5 year old girl voids normally but her underwear is always damp. Step 1: constant wetness despite normal voiding means some urine bypasses the bladder and its sphincter. Step 2: that implies a ureter opening below the external sphincter. Step 3: in girls, ectopic ureters usually come from a duplex system, and by the Weigert-Meyer rule the upper pole ureter is the one that ends low and medial. Step 4: imaging would therefore show a duplex kidney with a dilated, often poorly functioning upper pole draining into the urethra or vagina. A boy with the same anomaly would not leak, because his ectopic sites all lie above the external sphincter.

sections.title: Partition of the cloaca and remnants of the allantois

blocks.text: The cloaca is the endoderm lined chamber at the end of the hindgut. It receives the allantois, a diverticulum that extends into the connecting stalk, and the two mesonephric ducts, and it is closed ventrally by the cloacal membrane, where endoderm meets ectoderm without intervening mesoderm. Between about the fourth and seventh weeks, the urorectal septum, a wedge of mesoderm in the angle between the allantois and hindgut, grows toward the cloacal membrane and divides the cloaca in two.

blocks.title: Partition of the cloaca
steps: Urorectal septum grows caudally toward the cloacal membrane
Cloaca splits into urogenital sinus and anorectal canal
Cloacal membrane divides into urogenital and anal membranes
Septum tip forms the perineal body
Membranes rupture, opening the urogenital sinus and anus
blocks.caption: Partition is complete by about week 7; incomplete septation leaves fistulas between the rectum and the urinary or genital tract.

blocks.text: The urogenital sinus lies in front and forms the bladder and urethra; the anorectal canal lies behind and forms the rectum and upper anal canal. The sinus has three parts. The upper, vesical part becomes the bladder and is continuous at its apex with the allantois. The pelvic part becomes the prostatic and membranous urethra in males and the urethra in females. The phallic part becomes the spongy (penile) urethra in males and the vestibule in females. As the bladder grows, the caudal mesonephric ducts are absorbed into its posterior wall and form the trigone, with the ureters opening at its upper corners. The mesodermal lining of the trigone is soon replaced by endodermal epithelium, so the whole bladder lining is endodermal in the adult.

As the bladder enlarges, the lumen of the allantois is normally obliterated, leaving a thick fibrous cord, the urachus, which in the adult is the median umbilical ligament running from the bladder apex to the umbilicus along the inner abdominal wall. Persistence of all or part of the lumen produces a urachal anomaly, and the site of persistence predicts the finding.

blocks.title: Urachal anomalies
rows: The whole lumen, bladder to umbilicus
Clear urine leaking from the umbilicus, more when the bladder fills or strains
A middle segment, closed at both ends
Midline lower abdominal mass between umbilicus and bladder; may become infected
Outpouching at the bladder dome; may hold stagnant urine
blocks.caption: A patent vitelline (omphalomesenteric) duct, by contrast, drains bowel contents rather than urine at the umbilicus.

blocks.text: Two further points connect this section to others. A patent urachus is more likely when the bladder outlet is obstructed, as with posterior urethral valves, because sustained high bladder pressure keeps the channel open. Urachal remnants can also undergo glandular metaplasia, so cancers arising in them at the bladder dome are typically adenocarcinomas rather than the urothelial carcinomas that arise elsewhere in the bladder.

blocks.predict: A newborn has clear fluid leaking from the umbilicus that worsens when he cries. What structure failed to close, and how could you tell this fluid from the drainage of a patent vitelline duct?
blocks.explain: The allantois failed to obliterate (patent urachus), so bladder urine reaches the umbilicus; vitelline duct drainage is bowel content, not urine.

sections.title: Posterior urethral valves and lower tract obstruction

blocks.text: Posterior urethral valves are obstructing membranous folds in the posterior (prostatic) urethra, typically just distal to the verumontanum. They occur only in males, because they form in the male posterior urethra in relation to the entry of the mesonephric duct derivatives, and they are the most common cause of congenital bladder outlet obstruction in boys (about 1 in 5,000 to 8,000 male births). The folds act like a one way valve: urine flowing out balloons them into the lumen and blocks the stream, while a catheter passed retrograde slips through easily.

Because the obstruction sits below the bladder, the entire urinary tract above it is exposed to high pressure. The detrusor hypertrophies and becomes trabeculated as it pushes against the blocked outlet, and the bladder distends. The posterior urethra above the valves dilates. Raised bladder pressure is transmitted up both ureters, which dilate and become tortuous, and both renal pelves and calyces dilate: bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. Vesicoureteral reflux often coexists because the high pressure distorts the ureterovesical junctions.

blocks.title: Posterior urethral valves in the fetus
steps: Valves obstruct the male posterior urethra
Bladder pressure rises; detrusor thickens and bladder distends
Posterior urethra dilates above the valves
Backpressure dilates both ureters, pelves, and calyces
High pressure during nephrogenesis causes renal dysplasia
Fetal urine output falls: oligohydramnios
Pulmonary hypoplasia and Potter features
blocks.caption: Outlet obstruction affects both kidneys at once, unlike a unilateral ureteropelvic junction obstruction.

blocks.text: The damage begins before birth. Obstruction during nephrogenesis distorts branching and induction, so the kidneys may be dysplastic and the total nephron number reduced, a loss that is not reversed when the obstruction is relieved. As the kidneys fail, fetal urine output falls, oligohydramnios follows, and the same Potter sequence seen in renal agenesis can develop, with pulmonary hypoplasia as the main threat to life. The severity of oligohydramnios and how early it appears therefore track the severity of renal injury.

These mechanisms explain the diagnostic findings. Prenatal ultrasound in a male fetus shows a distended, thick walled bladder, a dilated posterior urethra (often called the keyhole sign), bilateral hydroureteronephrosis, and reduced amniotic fluid. After birth, an infant may have a palpable bladder, a weak or dribbling stream, urinary tract infection, and rising serum creatinine; a voiding cystourethrogram shows the dilated posterior urethra above the valves. Damaged tubules often cannot concentrate urine or acidify it well, so polyuria and acidosis can persist even after the outlet is opened.

blocks.title: Distinguishing congenital obstruction by level
rows: Incomplete canalization, crossing lower pole vessel
Usually unilateral pelvis and calyces; normal ureter
Ureter and kidney on the affected side
blocks.caption: Dilation stops at the level of obstruction; only a block below the bladder affects both kidneys and the bladder together.

blocks.title: Worked example: locating the obstruction
blocks.text: A fetal ultrasound at 24 weeks shows a male fetus with a large, thick walled bladder, dilation of both ureters and both renal pelves, and markedly low amniotic fluid. Step 1: both kidneys are affected, so the block lies where the two systems share a path, at or below the bladder. Step 2: the bladder itself is distended and thickened, which places the block below it, at the outlet or urethra. Step 3: in a male fetus the classic cause is posterior urethral valves. Step 4: low amniotic fluid means fetal urine output has fallen, which signals kidney injury and predicts pulmonary hypoplasia. A unilateral ureteropelvic junction obstruction would leave the bladder and amniotic fluid normal.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain the adult urinary tract. The split between bud and mesenchyme defines where the nephron ends and the collecting duct begins. The arterial ladder of ascent explains accessory renal arteries, and the absorption of the mesonephric duct into the bladder explains the trigone, the position of the ureteric orifices, and the shared urinary and genital anomalies in both sexes. Genetics links induction failure to RET and WT1, and karyotype abnormalities such as Turner syndrome to fusion anomalies.

Physiology and pathology explain the consequences. The fetus relies on the placenta for excretion and on its own kidneys for amniotic fluid, so renal failure before birth shows up as oligohydramnios and pulmonary hypoplasia rather than uremia. After birth, obstruction and reflux cause stasis, ascending infection, and scarring, and any loss of nephrons during nephrogenesis is permanent because no new nephrons form after about week 36.

summary: Pronephros (week 4, nonfunctional), mesonephros (late week 4, interim), and metanephros (week 5, permanent) arise in sequence from intermediate mesoderm.
The metanephros makes urine from about weeks 10 to 12, and fetal urine is the main source of amniotic fluid from mid pregnancy.
GDNF from metanephric mesenchyme acting on RET of the ureteric bud drives branching, and bud signals induce nephron formation.
The bud forms the ureter, pelvis, calyces, and collecting ducts; the mesenchyme forms Bowman capsule through the distal convoluted tubule.
Failed induction causes renal agenesis; bilateral agenesis causes oligohydramnios and Potter sequence with fatal pulmonary hypoplasia.
Horseshoe kidney forms when the lower poles fuse, and its isthmus is trapped under the inferior mesenteric artery; it is linked to Turner syndrome.
Early bud splitting gives a bifid ureter; two buds give a duplex ureter, in which the upper pole ureter obstructs or is ectopic and the lower pole ureter refluxes.
An ectopic ureter below the external sphincter in a girl causes constant dribbling with normal voiding.
The urorectal septum divides the cloaca into urogenital sinus and anorectal canal; failed obliteration of the allantois leaves a patent urachus or urachal cyst.
Posterior urethral valves in boys cause a distended thick walled bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis, renal dysplasia, and oligohydramnios.

verify: Timing values (pronephros early week 4, mesonephros late week 4 to end of month 2, ascent complete by about week 9, metanephric urine from about weeks 10 to 12, nephrogenesis ending about weeks 34 to 36) differ slightly between Langman, Moore, and review sources; confirm what NABNE expects.

Prevalence figures (horseshoe kidney about 1 in 400 to 600, accessory renal arteries about 25%, posterior urethral valves about 1 in 5,000 to 8,000 male births) are approximate and vary by source; renal agenesis frequencies were deliberately not given because published values differ widely.
Signaling detail beyond GDNF and RET (WT1 competence, WNT9B and FGF signals from the bud) follows Langman and current developmental biology; confirm the depth NABNE Part I tests.
The origin of mesangial cells (metanephric stromal lineage) is stated as current consensus but is described differently in older texts.
The embryologic origin of posterior urethral valves is debated; this chapter states only that they form in the male posterior urethra near the entry of mesonephric duct derivatives.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Weigert-Meyer rule, Potter sequence, Wolffian duct, and Gartner duct, or only the descriptive terms.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: nephrogenesis (ureteric bud branching into metanephric mesenchyme with renal vesicle to S shaped tubule), kidney-ascent (pelvic to lumbar position with arterial ladder and horseshoe kidney under the inferior mesenteric artery), duplex-ureter (Weigert-Meyer crossing and orifice positions), and cloaca-partition (urorectal septum dividing the cloaca, with allantois and urachus).
